doc.title: Butch Cage and Robert Pete Williams Interview, 1967-05-13
doc.interviewee: Butch Cage and Robert Pete Williams

chapter: Williams on guitar technique and prison
title: Release to Rudolph Eastley, the governor, and giving up playing for suppers
summary: Williams tells how Eastley took him from camp to his place above Zachary, where he played for the governor, and why he now declines to play out; he recalls 1932 wages.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: And I was standing up on my head. It wasn't a little ahead up there. I felt it good. So, when my partner come and released me that morning. I went on to the camp and I told the boy, I said, well, I'm going to tell all you fellas something. What you got to tell us this morning? I said, I ain't going to be here with y'all long. He said, oh, man, hush that racket. You know better than that. I said, okay. I said, just watch it. Well, I pulled my clothes off and I went to bed. I lay on my face. Somebody come in and they shut me. Just as I was slumming off to sleep. Said, they want you at the office somewhere. I got him, put the clothes on, went on over to the office. Well, that's Mr. Barnett over there. He come over there to get my record at Camp H over there. Mm-hmm. Well, they said, what you got to do with his record? He ain't been here no time. He said, forget about that. How long he been here? He said, I want you the record. He said, okay, okay. Well, they give him my record. He said, oh, Robert Peake. He said, you think I'll get away from here? You know that? I said, no, sir. I didn't know it. He said, that's right. I said, I'm glad of it. He said, I'm glad of it. So, and next, well, Mr. Barnett, I mean, Mr. Rudolph Eastley came. He said, I never seen you before, and I don't know you. I don't know you by your record. He said, you got a good record. And I see you ain't nothing but a phone man. And he said, I'm going to get you on my phone. Will you go? I told him, yes, sir. The man said, well, I ain't came you today. He said, well, I'll be back a few more days to get you. Well, he did, like he said, come up in there and got me and carried me up to his place up there above Zachary. And after we got there, well, that's when we met the governor and his two friends. I had my guitar. The governor made me come on into Mr. Rudolph's daughter's house. They made coffee and gave me coffee and told me to play the guitar, and I played. And even I rode in the car with the governor. And I rode down and looked at his Mr. Rudolph Eastley's hogs, cows, and everything. And I rode down there. And ever since then, and it helped some go that I've been out. But that's the very reason I don't go nowhere now, as you all asked me, did I get any plays out? Well, I would go out and play just like if the white folks would come get me, you know, and take me out like I was playing at the LSU because there's no trouble. But like, every cause of my trouble, what I got into, I was misused for another man. That's why I was in trouble. Misused for another man. So I promised the good Lord that I wasn't going out playing for no suppers no more. And I don't do it now. They wanted me over here, see, we're back with Tash for Hope. And I told them no, we're coming. Because these fellas get to drinking that wine, and throwing balls, and ask me why you come from. It's so many people that favors you. So, you tell them why you came from with that old bleeding. And just like you and the madam over there, and you, up there was it. If somebody in New York favors you, if somebody in Newport favors you later there, if somebody in San Francisco favors you, if someone in Texas favors you, everywhere favors them. That's to be thought of. Well, that's just the way the world runs. But, I would come back on this to say this. I have seen some hard times in my days. I do know the time in 32, I mean my mother. We used to work for, my mother was getting 25 cents a day, and I was getting 50 cents. But when the weapon run out, you didn't have nothing to do. We was working for a millionaire or two. You know him, that's Mr. Hughes. Yeah, yeah, he was.
